uncited: Multi-scale filtering refers to a family of techniques in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that mitigate aliasing artifacts and optimize rendering performance by adapting the Gaussian representation to the camera's viewing frequency or resolution.
All methods in this family address the mismatch between the discrete sampling of the image sensor and the continuous representation of 3D Gaussians.
The core mechanism involves modifying the projected 2D covariance matrix $\Sigma_{2D}$ to account for the sampling frequency or pixel size.
**Covariance Regularization:** To prevent aliasing (high-frequency artifacts) when zooming out or rendering at low resolution, a low-pass filter is applied.
**Opacity Preservation:** Adding variance spreads the Gaussian, reducing its peak height.
**Frequency Matching:** The filter parameters are tuned to match the Nyquist limit of the rendering resolution.
For training-time methods, this involves constraining the 3D representation frequency to the training data's sampling rate .
For test-time methods, it involves adapting to the specific camera distance and resolution .

The problem of aliasing in 3D Gaussian Splatting arises because standard 3DGS systematically underestimates the scale parameter during optimization, leading to erosion effects when zooming in and high-frequency artifacts when zooming out .
MIP-Splatting  was introduced to address these resolution-dependent artifacts by integrating multi-scale representations.
The theoretical basis relies on treating the camera sensor as a box filter and ensuring the Gaussian's spectral content does not exceed the Nyquist limit of the sampling grid .
